issues.legal_issue: A natural drainage phenomenon may be treated as having occurred from time immemorial when its precise commencement cannot be fixed and the evidence shows that it was known to have occurred for a long period.
material_facts: The lower appellate court found that flood water had flowed northward through the lands in the usual course of nature from time immemorial.

After remand, the appellate court referred to approximate years when the drainage arrangements existed but did not find that the phenomenon began in either year, and could not fix its precise commencement.
The High Court reversed the lower courts’ decrees, and the matter came before the Supreme Court in a civil appeal.
issues.conclusion: The evidence supported the inference that the phenomenon had occurred from time immemorial; the lower appellate court’s finding on that point stood.
issues.legal_principle: A phenomenon is from time immemorial when its commencement is outside human memory or shrouded in antiquity. If the available evidence does not establish the precise year in which it began, the proper inference is that it was known to occur from time immemorial, provided the evidence shows it had been occurring for a considerable period.

predicates.civil_appeal_challenges_reversal: A party brings a civil appeal challenging a judgment that reversed a lower court’s finding about a longstanding phenomenon.
predicates.phenomenon_known_for_long_period: The evidence shows that the phenomenon was known to occur over a considerable period.
predicates.precise_commencement_cannot_be_fixed: The evidence does not establish the precise time when the phenomenon began.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal challenges a reversed finding, a phenomenon known over a considerable period with no ascertainable precise beginning is treated as having occurred from time immemorial.

issues.legal_issue: A landowner may not obstruct the natural drainage of ordinary periodic flood water where the obstruction prevents the water from following its natural course.
material_facts: The lands lay in a basin from which surplus water ordinarily drained northward through a natural outlet.
When the receiving drain was in spate, flood water flowed northward, and the lower appellate court found this occurred every year in the usual course of nature and had occurred from time immemorial.
The landowners erected a bund and dug trenches that prevented the water from flowing northward, causing it to stagnate on the adjoining land and damage crops.
The lower appellate court found that the floods were not unusual, abnormal, occasional, or extraordinary.
issues.conclusion: The bund and trenches were wrongful because they impeded the natural flow of periodic flood water; the appellant was entitled to the relief claimed.
issues.legal_principle: Illustration (1) to section 7 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, permits the owner of higher land to pass water onto lower land, including flood water where flooding is usual or periodic in the locality. A landowner cannot obstruct a natural outlet by impeding water’s natural flow. The Court relied on Nield v. London & North Western Railway for the limitation on preventing natural drainage and referred to Menzies v. Breadalbane in discussing the rule concerning flow along a natural course. Even a riparian owner’s protection against extraordinary floods does not authorize impeding a stream’s natural course.

predicates.natural_drainage_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a landowner may interfere with water draining along its natural course onto or across other land.
predicates.flood_occurs_usually_or_periodically: Flood water reaches the land as a usual or periodic occurrence rather than as an extraordinary event.
predicates.obstruction_blocks_natural_flow: A landowner creates an obstruction that prevents the water from following its natural course and outlet.

issues.definition: In a natural-drainage dispute, an obstruction that blocks the usual or periodic natural flow of flood water is wrongful.
